title: British hacker who stole $11m jailed for six years in US
description: A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message
body: A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims.Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, started hacking as a teenager and was part of the collective of young hackers known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high profile cyber-crimes.US prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims and showed the growing threat posed by online crime groups.The sentence brings to an end a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada.Buchanan admitted taking part in a hacking campaign that began in 2021, when he was 19.Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.It made them $8m in less than two years, according to US prosecutors.Buchanan and his hacker gang sent out hundreds of SMS messages to the mobile phones of people who worked for large tech or telecoms companies.The SMS phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to look like legitimate sites of victim companies.The group used messages like "Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps".The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), and account usernames and passwords.The boys and young men did it on an industrial scale with Buchanan setting up a Telegram bot to collect all the victims' credentials as the duped workers unwittingly handed over their login details.For some victim companies, subsequently stolen information included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.The group then used stolen information and SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States.In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.Buchanan was also a victim of cyber-criminals.In early 2023 his online identity and home address were leaked by rival hackers seeking access to his cryptocurrency.Cyber security researchers and journalists reported that he was assaulted at his home and threatened with a blowtorch."TylerB and his group were highly sophisticated and organised but the violence he and others experienced was a sign of the troubling direction of these online communities of young hackers" says cyber security researcher Allison Nixon from Unit221B.Buchanan then reportedly fled to Canada to escape further threats before returning home.In April 2023, officers from Police Scotland searched Buchanan's bedroom after receiving a request from the FBI.Investigators recovered a device containing the names and addresses of hacking victims, along with cryptocurrency seed phrases and account credentials belonging to at least one victim.The following month, Buchanan left the UK again.He was arrested on 31 May 2024 at Palma de Mallorca Airport in Spain while attempting to board a private flight to Naples.After being extradited to the United States, he remained in custody before being sentenced this week.In his November 2023 charge, Buchanan was named along with four American men and boys in their twenties and teens for alleged activity linked to the notorious cyber-criminal collective Scattered Spider.They have all pleaded guilty too and are now serving time in jail.Two other members of the Scattered Spider group were jailed in the UK in July for various cyber attacks including a disruptive one against Transport for London that caused £39m of damage.

schema.headline: British hacker who stole $11m jailed for six years in US

title: Julio Iglesias faces court investigation over alleged sexual offences
description: Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff m
body: Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff membersTwo women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations.But in a statement published on Wednesday, external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio Piña said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment. But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. Piña said these allegations were dismissed after he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".Piña said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February. The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations. In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario, external and television network Univision news, published in January.In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions. The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.Rebeca, a Dominican who was 22 when the alleged events took place, also alleged that Iglesias had forced her to take part in threesomes with another female member of staff. She also described the singer slapping her in the face and grabbing her genitals.The other woman, a Venezuelan physical therapist named as Laura in the article, said Iglesias had touched her breasts and kissed her on the mouth against her will. She added that he constantly threatened to fire her, controlled how much food she ate and asked her about when her period was due.Rebeca and Laura filed an initial legal complaint in January against Iglesias for sexual assault and human trafficking.In a response to the allegations in January, Iglesias said, external: "I deny having abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and deeply sadden me."On Wednesday, the court said the lawsuit had been accepted based on evidence provided in the complaint. This included a photograph of one of the complainants, showing a bruise on her arm that was "consistent with the possibility of her being grabbed forcefully".It added that the same photo showed "two marks on one of her thighs that could correspond to a human bite", which the complainant said were "a consequence of her forced participation in acts of a sexual nature".WhatsApp message exchanges, including New Year's greetings, which suggest an "affectionate" relationship between the women and Iglesias, will also be considered, the court said.But it added that the seemingly cordial tone, which presents "an apparent discrepancy with certain aspects of the narrative", would be clarified through a "complete and contextualised examination of the communications".The claim over violations of workers' rights could not be investigated because there is no comparable criminal offence in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic, where the alleged crimes took place, it said.Iglesias is one of the most successful Latin artists of all time, having sold more than 300 million records in a career spanning decades.He is also the father of fellow music superstar Enrique Iglesias.

schema.headline: Julio Iglesias faces court investigation over alleged sexual offences

title: Grand Theft Auto VI: South Africa's DJ Lag features along Burna Boy, Asake in GTA 6
description: Rockstar Games, the developer behind the franchise, has revealed details of the game's soundtrack and some in-game radio stations, but has yet to rele
body: Rockstar Games, the developer behind the franchise, has revealed details of the game's soundtrack and some in-game radio stations, but has yet to release a complete list of songs featured in the game.Rockstar says AfroBank FM features everything from 20th Century African classics to contemporary amapiano and 3-step, giving the continent's music a prominent place in the latest edition.Burna Boy co-hosts the station alongside British DJ and producer Palms Trax, while Asake's hit song Joha is among the tracks players can listen to as they drive around the game's virtual world.DJ Lag, whose real name is Lwazi Asanda Gwala, is regarded as one of the pioneers of gqom, a genre of electronic dance music that emerged in the port city of Durban in the early 2010s.He posted on Instagram: "God did."Ghanaian highlife legends Pat Thomas and Ebo Taylor also feature, alongside South African artists Robot Boii and Kamo Mphela, bringing a mix of classic and contemporary African music to one of gaming's biggest franchises.Rockstar has also announced a 34-track official soundtrack album, released in partnership with Atlantic Records, featuring an original Burna Boy song titled Bigger.For African fans, the inclusion of familiar music adds another dimension to the experience, allowing players to hear some of the continent's biggest sounds while exploring the American setting.The series allows players to roam through sprawling fictional cities, drive vehicles and complete missions involving crime, police pursuits and other adventures.The latest instalment takes players to Vice City, a fictional version of Miami, and the surrounding US state of Leonida, inspired by Florida.Its story follows two criminals, Jason and Lucia, who become caught up in a wider conspiracy after a robbery goes wrong.The launch has generated enormous excitement among gamers around the world.Some fans downloaded it in advance so they could begin playing as soon as it became available, while others have booked leave from work.The previous edition, GTA 5, was one of the best-selling video games of all time, selling more than 200 million copies worldwide.The new release is expected to be another major commercial success, although it remains to be seen whether it will match its predecessor's extraordinary sales.

schema.headline: Grand Theft Auto VI: South Africa's DJ Lag features along Burna Boy, Asake in GTA 6

title: Senegal boat disaster: Dozens missing as boat with 100 migrants sinks
description: Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat reportedly carrying about 100 migrants capsized off the coast.Initial reports sai
body: Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat reportedly carrying about 100 migrants capsized off the coast.Initial reports said that one person had died, but some local media have reported that at least four bodies have been recovered. Dozens of people are still missing.Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT)."Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, AFP reported.Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.As it has become more difficult to reach Europe through North Africa, due to tighter controls and increased co-operation with European countries, migrants are increasingly targeting Spain's Canary Islands.They often travel in wooden boats known as pirogues that are frequently overloaded and not suited to such long voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.Most migrants arriving in the Canary Islands this year are from Senegal, according to the UN.They are driven to leave home by limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks, according to the IOM.On 7 November, El Hierro, one of the Canary Islands, declared a state of emergency following a surge in migrant arrivals.It said more than 3,300 people had reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. This amounts to almost a third of the island's population.

schema.headline: Senegal boat disaster: Dozens missing as boat with 100 migrants sinks

title: Putin's Crimean Bridge comes under attack again, Russian official says
description: Crimean Bridge attacked again, Russia saysFigure caption, Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack earlier this
body: Crimean Bridge attacked again, Russia saysFigure caption, Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack earlier this weekByClaire KeenanUpdated 4 hours agoThe Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, Russia has said.The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said that rail traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea.On Tuesday, Ukrainian missiles and drones destroyed the central road section of the critical bridge, collapsing part of it into the water.The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.Image source, ReutersImage caption, A screengrab of the damaged Crimean bridge in the Kerch Strait on 17 NovemberIt comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China.Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram.Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the attack, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge."As a result of a nighttime drone attack, train services on the railway section of the Crimean Bridge have been temporarily suspended," the ministry said in a statement on Telegram.Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.At least four people were killed in a Russian drone attack on the southern city of Odesa on Wednesday, according to Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road.That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line.Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days.Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.

schema.headline: Putin's Crimean Bridge comes under attack again, Russian official says

title: William and Kate meet PM Modi as they wrap up India tour
description: On Wednesday, William and Catherine travelled from Mumbai to capital New Delhi for the final leg of their trip.During a meeting at Modi's private resi
body: On Wednesday, William and Catherine travelled from Mumbai to capital New Delhi for the final leg of their trip.During a meeting at Modi's private residence, a Kensington Palace spokesperson said the royals and Modi discussed the "strength and importance of the UK–India bilateral relationship, reflecting on the deep and enduring ties between the two countries and the opportunities to strengthen their partnership in the years ahead".The prince and princess also spoke "warmly" of their time in the country, thanking the prime minister and the people for their welcome, and saying how much they enjoyed returning to India, a decade after their last visit.Modi called it a "pleasure" to meet them, and said he looks forward to "further strengthening" the UK–India partnership for the "shared prosperity of the people of our nations and the wider world".When Prince William announced earlier this year that The Earthshot Prize ceremony was going to be held in India for the first time, he highlighted India's leadership in climate innovation, its biodiversity and its massive youth population as the key reasons for choosing the country.The royal spokesperson said that the meeting with Modi touched on the success of the ceremony in Mumbai, and India's "growing leadership in environmental innovation".The event, founded by Prince William in 2020, was hosted this year by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known filmmakers.The couple last met the Indian prime minister on their official visit to India in 2016.

schema.headline: William and Kate meet PM Modi as they wrap up India tour

title: Falcon 6X: Why Ghana is facing backlash over new $60m presidential jet
description: Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.Par
body: Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.Parliament approved its purchase last December as part of a broader programme to modernise Ghana's military aviation fleet, which also includes four helicopters from Airbus.The jet was welcomed with a water salute on Monday, but its arrival triggered criticism online and among opposition politicians over the cost and timing of the purchase. While in the opposition, Mahama himself opposed buying a new presidential jet, prompting questions about why his administration has now gone head with the purchase.Opposition MP Samuel Abu Jinapor questioned the government's priorities, saying the expenditure came at a time when many Ghanaians continue to struggle with the cost of living and youth unemployment remained alarmingly high."What was unacceptable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government merely because the occupants of power have changed," Jinapor added. He accused the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) of hypocrisy, recalling how its senior figures had strongly opposed proposals for a new presidential aircraft when they were in opposition.Jinapor also called for greater transparency over the procurement process, how the purchase was financed and the government's justification for the expenditure.The purchase has also prompted sharp criticism on social media, with some users arguing the money could have been spent on more pressing public needs."This money can employ over 100,000 nurses and 200,000 teachers," an X user posted. But the government has rejected the criticism, saying Ghana's economic circumstances have changed considerably since the NDC opposed a similar purchase.Peter Lanchene Toobu, chairman of parliament's defence committee, said the party had never opposed acquiring a presidential jet in principle. Its objection, he said, had been on the timing when Ghana was experiencing severe economic difficulties."We agreed in principle that we needed to purchase a new presidential jet," he said.He argued, however, that Ghana could not justify the expenditure at a time when it was seeking a $3bn bailout from the IMF."The strength and macroeconomic stability of this country have enhanced our status in the sense that imports have become cheaper, and this is the right time," he added.Toobu said the government had purchased the aircraft without borrowing, citing a stronger Ghanaian currency and improved economic conditions.Government spokesperson Kwakye Ofosu also dismissed suggestions that the purchase was a misplaced priority.He pointed to falling prices of construction materials and lower borrowing costs as evidence of the country's improved economic situation."When I was campaigning in 2024, and I was donating cement, it cost 115 cedis (£7.5) a bag. Today, for 80 cedis, you will get a bag of cement," he told JoyNews.The controversy has also extended to the aircraft's interior, following claims that it has a dedicated bedroom and bathroom.But Ofosu dismissed claims that the jet had such luxury facilities, saying the president has no intention of "bathing in the air"."There certainly is no bathroom. President Mahama has no intention of bathing in the air," Ofosu said.He explained that the jet has reclining seats that can be converted into sleeping arrangements but denied that it has a dedicated bedroom.The government says the new jet will replace the 16-year-old Falcon 900EX, which has suffered recurring maintenance problems, including corrosion and leakages in its fuel tank.The older jet was reportedly grounded in France for several months in 2025 while undergoing repairs.Officials say the Falcon 6X has a longer flying range, reducing the need for refuelling stops on international trips and improving the reliability of presidential travel.Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin, an economist at the University of Ghana said that while the president's safety was paramount, the timing of the purchase was difficult to justify amid severe austerity measures, high unemployment and widespread infrastructure challenges."The timing makes it a bit difficult to understand," he told the BBC, adding that the government should provide a cost-benefit analysis explaining why buying the jet was preferable to leasing one and how the decision serves Ghana's interests.Additional reporting by Thomas Naadi in Accra

schema.headline: Falcon 6X: Why Ghana is facing backlash over new $60m presidential jet

title: Russian arrested for spying on US defence company Palantir over Ukraine support
description: A Russian man has been arrested in California's Silicon Valley for allegedly attempting to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm that supp
body: A Russian man has been arrested in California's Silicon Valley for allegedly attempting to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm that supports the Ukrainian military.Igor D'iu is accused of acting as an agent of a foreign government to conduct a covert operation in Palo Alto, near San Francisco. The BBC understands that the company targeted was Palantir Technologies. D'iu is also charged with stalking employees and possessing falsified identity documents. The company is not named in charging documents, but is described as a publicly traded technology and defence company that produces software used by Ukraine in its war with Russia."The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian."We will not tolerate any efforts - by foreign governments or otherwise - to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations."Prosecutors say that D'iu entered the US unlawfully via the Mexico border, after travelling there from Istanbul in June.He was allegedly recruited through the Telegram encrypted messaging app. His handlers referred to Russia as "'the Motherland' and directed D'iu to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine". On their instruction, he purchased computers, phones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software - tools he needed for his spy mission.He then went to a coffee shop located near the company's offices in Palo Alto, where he photographed laptop screens of employees who were working there. His handlers also allegedly "instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity".A source in the industry confirmed that Palantir was targeted, and added that the operation did not penetrate the company's private systems.They added that the company has been "targeted extensively" by Russia over its involvement in Ukraine, and that the attacks are becoming "increasingly aggressive".The source, who did not want to be named, said that this was the first time a Russian operative was found while on US soil attempting to spy on the company. "I think the surprising thing is that they decided to take the risk of sending someone to the US," they said, in an attempt to get into the system "physically". Palantir has not issued a statement in reaction to the charges.D'iu also allegedly conducted surveillance of employees and their residences. On 3 September, he followed a vehicle driven by one senior executive for nearly 30 miles. He fled after she drove to a police station. Police later obtained evidence that he had followed other employees' cars on previous days.During the investigation, officials discovered identity cards that had been falsified - including a US passport, California ID card, and a Social Security card with the fake name "Hugo Landry Johns".A raid on his home in October in East Palo Alto turned up two Russian passports, and a handwritten notebook that contained numerous home addresses of employees "family members' names, educational and employment histories, and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses", prosecutors say.He faces two charges related his alleged work as a foreign agent, one charge of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud related to his identity documents. He faces over 15 years in prison if found guilty.

schema.headline: Russian arrested for spying on US defence company Palantir over Ukraine support

title: Nvidia reports bumper results as firm says it's not reinstating Jensen Huang
description: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as it reports soaring salesImage source, Getty/Nvidia via ReutersImage caption, Jensen Huang and Nvidia's interim
body: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as it reports soaring salesImage source, Getty/Nvidia via ReutersImage caption, Jensen Huang and Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette KressByKali HaysTechnology reporter and Osmond ChiaBusiness reporterUpdated 18 November 2026Nvidia has firmly ruled out letting ousted co-founder Jensen Huang return as it revealed that sales doubled to more than $100bn.In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit last week, covering the three month period just before the recent scandal surfaced, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it was "business as usual". She told investors: "We've got this."Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.But Nvidia's chair Harvey Jones said: "The board does not intend to reinstate him."   Nvidia reported that sales for the three months to 25 October rose to $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading. The company's profits also doubled from a year ago rising to $65bn. Sales from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn.The company said its rapid growth is poised to continue and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance. Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader."The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."Figure caption, Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry."It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects"."Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."The interim chief executive also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection."With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new chief executive will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said.

schema.headline: Nvidia reports bumper results as firm says it's not reinstating Jensen Huang

title: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
description: Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ord
body: Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly announced by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.In the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.In the evening, the IDF said the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".On Thursday morning, Cogat told Palestinians on social media that "the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened".Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".Gaza's Hamas-run government media office meanwhile said that an estimated 6,000 people had fled their homes and tents because of the operation, and that this amounted to the war crime of forced displacement.Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed dozens of families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the Israeli evacuation order.In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man could be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he said.Automatic gunfire could be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter.""We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".Asked about those reports, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second was killed to the north in Gaza City, and the third was killed in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, its health ministry says.

schema.headline: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line

title: Pew survey: What India's changing Hindu and Muslim populations tell us
description: India's religious make-up - what a new Pew study says about Hindus and MuslimsImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, An Indian woman lights
body: India's religious make-up - what a new Pew study says about Hindus and MuslimsImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, An Indian woman lights lamps on the occasion of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lightsByIndia correspondentIndia will remain overwhelmingly Hindu for decades to come, but its religious composition is projected to shift gradually.A new study by the Pew Research Center, projecting the world's religious populations to 2070, estimates that Hindus will make up 76% of India's population by then, down from 79% in 2020, while the Muslim share will rise from 15% to 20%.The shift is rooted largely in differences in age and fertility: Indian Muslims are younger than Hindus and, on average, have more children.The Pew projections place India at the centre of a wider demographic shift across South Asia. Pakistan is expected to overtake Indonesia as the country with the world's largest Muslim-majority population, with India moving into second place. Bangladesh, too, is projected to see substantial growth in its Muslim population.The study projects the religious composition of the world over the next 50-year period, drawing on data from 201 countries and territories, covering virtually the entire global population.Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, Muslims offer prayer at the historic Jama Masjid in DelhiIt tracks seven religious groups between 2020 and 2070, assuming recent demographic trends continue. Using census and survey data, it establishes each group's size and age profile in 2020, and factors in differences in fertility and religious switching.The findings place India at the heart of a changing global religious landscape. The country is expected to have the world's second-largest Muslim population by 2070, after Pakistan, with about 334 million Muslims. Pakistan itself will overtake Indonesia as the country with the largest Muslim population, with an estimated 461 million.Yet the projections offer little support for the more dramatic narratives sometimes attached to India's changing religious composition. If current demographic trends continue, the Hindu population in the country is expected to grow by 176 million between 2020 and 2070, the report says. It will continue to account for more than three-quarters of the country's population. Despite a sharp fall in India's overall fertility, Muslim women still have more children, on average, than Hindu women. Pew attributes the shift primarily to demographic momentum. Indian Muslims had a median age of 24 in 2020, compared with 29 for Hindus. Between 2025 and 2030, Pew estimates Muslim women in India will have an average of 2.3 children, against 1.8 among Hindu women."We expect religious change in India to be driven almost entirely by long-standing demographic differences between Hindus and Muslims: Muslims are younger and have higher fertility rates," Stephanie Kramer of the Pew Research Center told the BBC.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Hindu devotees offer prayers on the banks of the Sabarmati river in India's Gujarat"The fertility gap has narrowed considerably – from more than one child per woman in 1992 to about half a child in recent years and is likely to keep shrinking," she said."But Hindu fertility is already below the replacement level, while Muslim fertility is projected to remain above it for another two decades." (A replacement level is one at which new births are sufficient to maintain a stable population.)The projections are hardly surprising, says KS James, an Indian demographer at Princeton University."The fertility gap between Muslims and Hindus is well established and it means Muslim population growth is likely to remain faster for the next few decades. But fertility is declining across all religious communities and the gap is expected to narrow further," he told the BBC."Ultimately, they will converge," he says, adding that the projections do not point to anything dramatically different in India's demographic trajectory.Demographers push back against claims, often amplified by Hindu right-wing groups, that Muslims will eventually outnumber Hindus. There is no evidence of any significant religious conversion driving population change in India, they say, and the projections do not support such "alarmist scenarios". Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, Muslim children dressed in festive attire in IndiaThe wider South Asian picture is equally revealing, according to the report. Pakistan's Muslim population is projected to more than double to 461 million by 2070, overtaking Indonesia as the world's largest. India will rank second, with 334 million Muslims, while Bangladesh's Muslim population will rise to 218 million. India and Nepal, meanwhile, will remain the world's only Hindu-majority countries.There appears to be a global story behind these regional shifts.By 2035, Muslims are projected to overtake Christians as the world's largest religious group, according to the report. By 2070, their numbers are expected to reach 3.64 billion, up from 2.02 billion in 2020. Christianity, meanwhile, will have just under three billion followers. Muslims will account for 36% of humanity, compared with 26% today.But the most dramatic transformation may be taking place thousands of miles west of South Asia, in Africa. Christianity's centre of gravity is moving steadily away from Europe and the Americas towards sub-Saharan Africa. The report says that if recent trends continue, more than half of the world's Christians are expected to live there by 2070, compared with 31% in 2020. Pew forecasts that the Democratic Republic of Congo will overtake the United States as the country with the largest Christian population.Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Images)Image caption, With more than 1.4 billion people, India overtook China in 2023 in terms of population, according to the UNThe steepest decline is expected to occur in Europe. If current trends continue, by 2070 Europe will be home to 11% of the world's Christian population, down from 22% in 2020, the report says.The US is projected to lose its Christian majority by 2065, although Christians will remain the country's largest religious group in 2070. One reason for this changing religious landscape is the growing number of people identifying with no religion.In UK and France, the "religiously unaffiliated" are projected to become the majority by 2070. South Korea is expected to follow suit. Yet their share of the world's population is forecast to fall from 24% to 17%, largely because of a decline in China's population.China accounts for about two-thirds of the world's religiously unaffiliated population. Its expected population decline will more than offset growth in secular populations elsewhere, the report says.By 2070, there are other unexpected shifts. The US is projected to become the world's fifth-largest Hindu population, with immigration driving much of its growth. And Australia's unaffiliated population will overtake Christians as the country's largest group. Buddhism, meanwhile, faces a demographic squeeze. Its population is expected to fall by more than half in China, Japan and South Korea, reflecting the ageing and shrinking populations of East Asia. Laos and Mongolia are projected to lose their Buddhist majorities.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Muslims offer Eid prayers in Pakistan There are, of course, caveats. These are demographic projections, not predictions of everything that might happen. Pew assumes that recently observed patterns of fertility, migration and religious switching - or conversions -  will continue."There are many events that could affect religious group populations (including wars, natural disasters, epidemics and changes in economic or social circumstances) that are not analysed here," the report admits.India's baseline also required projecting the 2020 religious composition from the 2011 census, because the subsequent census had been delayedStill, the broad direction is unmistakable. South Asia will remain indispensable to the world's religious story, not just because of India's enormous Hindu population but because of the growing weight of its Muslim populations. Africa will increasingly shape Christianity's future, while Europe and parts of East Asia become more secular.Clearly, by 2070, the world's religious landscape may look markedly different, shaped less by conversion than by the uneven arithmetic of births, deaths and migration.

schema.headline: Pew survey: What India's changing Hindu and Muslim populations tell us

title: Australia sandpapergate: Cameron Bancroft claims whole team knew of plot in South Africa
description: Cameron Bancroft has claimed the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current c
body: Cameron Bancroft has claimed the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.In a detailed testimony, published by the West Australian,, external batter Bancroft - the player caught with the sandpaper during the Test match against South Africa - has given arguably the most complete account of the events in Cape Town eight years ago."In 2018 not the entire truth was told," said Bancroft. "I have never been completely honest about what happened."For the past two weeks, Australian cricket has been embroiled in a debate over the ball-tampering saga following the publication of Usman Khawaja's autobiography.Khawaja wrote that the whole Australia team knew of the plot, claims supported by David Warner and Chadd Sayers. Cummins described Khawaja's account as "wrong" and "nonsense".On the day Cricket Australia announced a forum into the sandpaper episode, Bancroft published his account, explaining he was motivated by the news conference given by Cummins."The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," said Bancroft."It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone."What I saw, experienced and lived with - not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa - is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time."Khawaja's autobiography and the subsequent claims made by Warner and seamer Sayers have reopened old wounds related to the sandpaper saga.Still, those connected have remained true to the accounts they have presented during the intervening eight years.The most significant denial came from Cummins, who rebuffed Khawaja's account in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney. Lehmann and Starc have also reiterated their denials.Now, it is the extensive detail provided by Bancroft that could shed a whole new light on the controversy and lead to further questions for Cummins, Lehmann and Cricket Australia.Cummins is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand on 9 December.A statement released on behalf of Cummins said: "Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he's been through there's nothing in the statement that hasn't been answered by Pat in his press conference."A Cricket Australia statement said: "We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments."We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events."We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible."In his account, Bancroft said: "I have spent eight years speaking about accountability, honesty and the lessons I learned from one of Australian cricket's darkest moments."However, in 2018 not the entire truth was told. I have never been completely honest about what happened."It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team."When I was questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account."I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others."I did this to protect Cricket Australia's investigation and not implicate others around me."Bancroft said his actions were "discussed" and "acknowledged" by the entire playing group at the end of the second day and before the beginning of the third day. He said he was encouraged by Saker, who has since worked as a consultant with England.The only person within the camp to express unease at the ball-tampering, according to Bancroft, was media manager Kate Hutchison."I received wraps and encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff, especially David Saker," said Bancroft."Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening."I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion."I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up."Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it."Bancroft identifies Saker as the coach Khawaja claimed encouraged him to work harder on the ball during the third Test in Cape Town. The 33-year-old said he took "feedback" from all the bowlers and wicketkeeper Tim Paine, who took over the captaincy when Smith was sacked.In Cape Town, Bancroft was confronted by the umpires when TV cameras showed him concealing the sandpaper in his trousers. He claimed Lehmann sent a message to him via Handscomb."Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break after I'd been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants," wrote Bancroft."He said to me: 'I think it's time I take that off you now.' And Pete was doing his job after Boof [Lehmanm] shouted to him on the walkie talkie "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now"."If he didn't know he wouldn't have said that. And if it wasn't clear enough before, then it was obvious now."In 2021, Bancroft was playing county cricket with Durham and gave an interview to The Guardian in which he said the bowlers' involvement in the plot was "self-explantory".In response, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon released a joint-statement denying any knowledge that ball-tampering had taken place."Reading that statement was deeply painful," said Bancroft."I had memories of conversations on the field in Port Elizabeth and Newlands, feedback about the ball and shared celebrations that made the statement difficult for me to digest."For almost two weeks, Australian cricket has been at war with itself over the revelations in Usman Khawaja's autobiography.But there has been an absence of a smoking gun. Without tangible, new, hard evidence, all that was left was claim and counter-claim.Naturally, the spotlight fell on Pat Cummins because of his role as a bowler in Cape Town and his elevation to Australia captain in the years since.His performance last week in front of the media, on live television, was extraordinary. For 68 minutes he took all questions and appeared plausible in his answers.In being so robust in his denial of Khawaja's account - Cummins called it "nonsense" - the skipper also left himself open to the consequences if it was later revealed he was not telling the truth.Crucially, it was Cummins' press conference that compelled Cameron Bancroft to speak out.It must be stressed that Bancroft's account is not the open-and-shut evidence that convicts Cummins or anyone else in the dressing room at Newlands in 2018.But it is certainly the most complete account we have heard from anyone involved, walking step-by-step through the genesis of the plot, the execution and the fallout. Bancroft has named names: Cummins, the other bowlers, Tim Paine, coach Darren Lehmann and assistant coach David Saker. It is, potentially, the decisive intervention that shifts this whole saga in a new direction.Whether by accident or design, it came on the day Cricket Australia (CA) announced its forum for evidence into the sandpaper controversy. Before Bancroft's account CA's action felt an unsatisfactory halfway house - not an investigation, with no guarantee outcomes will be published.What now? Will CA go further? How will those implicated by Bancroft respond? How can Cummins lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand? Could Steve Smith break a silence he has held since the publication of Khawaja's book?Throughout the past fortnight, there has been a sense that Australian cricket hoped the sandpaper debate would eventually go away. Cummins even said he never wanted to speak about it again.Instead of fading, the thirst for the truth grows, now fuelled by Bancroft's extraordinary story.

schema.headline: Australia sandpapergate: Cameron Bancroft claims whole team knew of plot in South Africa

title: Lobito Corridor: Can Trump-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo and Angola?
description: As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not th
body: As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments.She is thinking about getting around more easily.The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast. For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient."Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport.It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo.Under agreements brokered by US President Donald Trump, DR Congo and neighbouring Rwanda have committed to greater economic cooperation, including more transparent mineral supply chains and regional infrastructure development.The wider plan envisages linking these initiatives to the railway, which transports minerals from Central Africa to Western markets via Angola, rather than east to China as most do currently.The hope is that formalising the mineral trade and encouraging investment could help curb illicit markets that have helped finance armed groups and fuel instability.But can a railway built to move minerals to global markets also deliver peace and prosperity?The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito.Its importance has grown as demand for copper and cobalt rises, driven partly by the global transition to cleaner energy, as both are critical ingredients for all kinds of electrical components."The timing matters," says Johannesburg-based political risk analyst Wellington Muzengeza"Electrification and the energy transition have increased the strategic importance of copper, cobalt and reliable mineral supply chains."DR Congo is the world's largest producer of cobalt and one of its biggest copper producers, along with neighbouring Zambia. The US sees the corridor as a means to diversify mineral supplies and reduce reliance on China, which dominates much of the world's processing capacity.A US-DR Congo strategic partnership identifies the route from the Congolese town of Sakania to Lobito as a priority for mineral exports, while the economic framework agreed by DR Congo and Rwanda envisages connecting regional infrastructure and trade initiatives to the corridor.The project has attracted over $750m (£570m), including funding backed by the US International Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa to upgrade railway tracks, signalling systems and trains.The railway, built in 1902 under Portuguese colonial rule, was originally designed to transport goods and minerals from Central Africa to the Atlantic coast. After years of disruption during Angola's civil war, it was rebuilt and fully reopened in 2015.The US first got involved in the project under former President Joe Biden but backing has continued under Trump.At Lobito's mineral terminal, the renewed ambitions are already visible.When the BBC visited, a train carrying about 12,000 tonnes of copper cathodes from DR Congo had arrived. Workers moved the refined copper sheets into a warehouse before they were loaded on to ships bound for international markets, mostly the US.The cargo is handled by Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), which has a 30-year concession to operate freight services along the corridor and manage the mineral terminal.Chief operating officer Nicholas Gregoir says freight volumes have more than doubled since the company took over in January 2024.LAR expects to transport about 200,000 tonnes of copper through the corridor in 2026.For mining companies, the railway offers a shorter route to international markets."The Lobito Corridor is the shortest route for both Zambia and the DRC," to the Atlantic, says Kátila Vanessa Monteiro da Silva Neto, executive director of the Lobito Port Authority.Zambia, Africa's second-largest copper producer, also plans to connect its Copperbelt to Lobito through a proposed 830km (515 mile)-railway.But a more efficient route to market does not automatically translate into economic transformation."Joining a corridor is not the same as industrialising," Muzengeza says. "The test is not simply whether Zambia gains another route to the sea. It is whether that route helps build a stronger economy."Some Angolans believe the railway's greatest value could lie in what it offers businesses and communities beyond mining."I call it a corridor of development," says businessman Adérito Areias.The railway passes through some of Angola's most productive agricultural regions. Better transport links could help farmers reach larger markets and reduce losses."If there isn't an artery carrying products from the interior to where there is demand, those products simply rot where they are produced," Areias says.But the challenge is turning that ambition into reality.The Port of Lobito handled about 1.8 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, of which around 158,000 tonnes was minerals. Its mineral terminal can handle up to 3.6 million tonnes annually."The port already has the capacity," says Neto. "What we need now is sufficient railway capacity and rolling stock."For residents along the route, the benefits have been immediate.State-owned railway operator Caminho de Ferro de Benguela (CFB), which runs passenger services, carried a record 1.6 million passengers in 2025.LAR says it directly employs nearly 1,000 people, 98% of them Angolan."This job allows me to support my family," says Domingos Canhama, a father of four and a forklift operator at CFB."I can put food on the table, maintain a home and help support my father," he says.Muzengeza argues that the bigger opportunity is developing local businesses in engineering, maintenance, warehousing and agricultural processing."Businesses in Angola need access to the railway, not just proximity to it. That means feeder roads, electricity, storage and predictable services," he says.But can minerals and their movement along the railways line help deliver peace to eastern DR Congo, where the battle for control of mineral resources has fuelled decades of conflict?Most recently, this has seen the M23 rebel group seize control of many mineral-rich areas. The Congolese government says neighbouring Rwanda is backing the M23 in order to gain access to DR Congo's mineral wealth. Despite overwhelming evidence, Rwanda denies backing the M23.The Trump-backed agreements between DR Congo and Rwanda seek to promote transparent mineral supply chains, cross-border investment and regional infrastructure, with the aim of ensuring mineral wealth does not finance armed groups."The US wants reliable access to minerals essential to defence, advanced technology and energy systems, while reducing dependence on supply chains in which China has substantial influence," says Muzengeza, the political risk analyst"Lobito is therefore more than a railway but an infrastructure that can reshape trade routes and commercial power."At a meeting in Paris in November, DR Congo urged the US to turn its strategic partnership into tangible investments, arguing that success should be measured by completed projects rather than signed agreements."We want the partnership to support ⁠local mineral processing, electricity access for households and businesses and peace in the east," said DR Congo's Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba.Even if more minerals move through formal channels, better infrastructure alone would not resolve the political and security tensions driving the conflict.There is also the question of who captures the wealth. Much of the copper and cobalt transported from DR Congo through Lobito is destined for processing and manufacturing outside Africa.While Angola can earn transit fees and create logistics jobs, much of the higher-value activity takes place elsewhere."When you export raw materials, you are also exporting jobs and knowledge," Angola's Foreign Affairs Minister Téte António tells the BBC.Areias shares that concern. "We should not export lithium but export batteries," he says, arguing that the corridor should help develop local processing and manufacturing rather than simply accelerate raw material exports.Back in Catumbela, such debates can feel distant from everyday life. For Julia, the railway already means cheaper journeys and easier movement.But its ultimate success will depend on whether it can deliver more than faster mineral exports.Whether it can also help secure lasting peace in eastern DR Congo, where the minerals are mined, remains the bigger test.

schema.headline: Lobito Corridor: Can Trump-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo and Angola?

title: Hakeem Jeffries nominated to be US Speaker of the House
description: Democrats in the US House of Representatives officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker, setting him on the path to become the first black law
body: Democrats in the US House of Representatives officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker, setting him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber.The House will elect its new Speaker on 3 January, when the next term begins and Democrats will be in the majority. His election to the powerful position - the Speaker is in line to succeed the president after the vice-president - is widely expected. Should he win, Jeffries will preside over his party's largest House majority in years and benefit from the Senate also being under Democrats' control.Jeffries told reporters after the vote that the nomination was "a high honour and a distinct privilege".As of Wednesday, Democrats will hold at least 257 seats in the House next year, which is well beyond the 218 needed for a majority. Seven races from the recent midterm elections are still uncalled. Jeffries, who represents a district in New York, was re-elected as the party leader in a 251-11 closed-door vote on Wednesday. He has served as minority leader since 2023.The Congressional Black Caucus, currently made up of only Democratic House members, noted the potential history-making moment when Jeffries takes the helm of the House."The American people, largely driven by turnout among Black communities, particularly across the south, have trusted us to make Washington work for them," said the committee's chair, Yvette Clarke, in a statement. "Now, it is our charge and responsibility to do all we can to deliver on their faith."Despite overwhelming support in Wednesday's vote , Jeffries faced a handful of holdouts from new members in the party's left wing, who have said the party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections is a sign voters want change."While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes in this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of our leadership," seven incoming lawmakers, including fellow New Yorkers Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, said in a statement.All congressional Democrats are gearing up for clashes with the White House once they officially take control in January.President Donald Trump, a Republican, has signalled a willingness to work with Democrats on some issues, but has also pledged to use his veto power to reject legislation he does not like. Trump's opposition could make it hard for Democrats to deliver on their campaign promises to address affordability and pass other reforms. At a news conference following the vote on Wednesday, Jeffries pledged that House Democrats would "fight to lower the high costs of groceries and gas and housing", and "make healthcare affordable for every single American".Though the party will have a large enough majority to weather defections on must-pass legislation, Jeffries will still have to navigate internal ideological divisions that have grown particularly sharp over US support of Israel and Americans' rising healthcare costs.Many incoming Democrats, including members of the Democratic Socialists of America, won their elections by challenging the party establishment.The Congressional Progressive Caucus, from the party's left wing, congratulated Jeffries on the nomination, adding they would "continue conversations with Leader Jeffries to ensure Democrats deliver a bold agenda for working people". Along with shepherding legislation, Jeffries as Speaker will also have to manage the complex array of investigations that Democrats plan to launch into Trump, his family, and cabinet members now that they have regained control of the chamber's oversight powers.Rounding out their party leadership team, House Democrats also elected Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as majority leader, Pete Aguilar of California as majority whip, and Joe Neguse of Colorado as assistant speaker.

schema.headline: Hakeem Jeffries nominated to be US Speaker of the House

title: Van Gogh painting sells for $190.4m after row over Nazi history
description: It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a
body: It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment. "In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.Four other owners then had the painting.The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

schema.headline: Van Gogh painting sells for $190.4m after row over Nazi history
